results.title: Scientific Data Analysis Pipelines and Reproducibility
results.content:
Title: Scientific Data Analysis Pipelines and Reproducibility
# Scientific Data Analysis Pipelines and Reproducibility | by Altuna Akalin | TDS Archive | Medium. # Scientific Data Analysis Pipelines and Reproducibility. How can one install the exact same pipeline with the exact dependencies its creator using and make sure it produces the same output? In addition, you need to know exact versions and configurations of the dependencies to have a shot at reproducing the data analysis pipeline. This will remain so even if we are promised to get a working pipeline that reproduces the authors version after we go through installation of each dependency diligently. If you can install the same exact software, built the same way with exactly the same dependencies down to the compiler, you have good chances at reproducing the runtime environment across different machines and therefore the analysis with the same input data. Reproducibility requires availability of data and being able to use the same exact software. In practical terms, what many of us have in mind when we want to use a published data analysis tool is the following : 1) “can I install the published software at all and get similar results ? I think answering these questions positively requires strict control of the dependencies of the data analysis pipeline. Or they should make sure when users install the pipeline they get identical versions of the dependencies. This means that if you can manage to install your pipeline and dependencies in this light-weight virtual machine, you can ship the container and be sure that anyone who uses that container will be able to reproduce your software environment. If you can make sure the installed software is identical bit-by-bit on different systems, you can have runtime reproducibility and have the same results with same input data (minus the caveats mentioned in “_Runtime environment reproducibility_” subsection). For the reproducibility and robustness it provides, we opted to use Guix to manage dependencies of our pipelines. Making the data analysis pipelines reproducible should be the aim for the scientists if they want their tools or approach to be used by a wider audience.

results.title: Why Should We Pay Attention To Reproducibility In Analysis Pipelines?
results.content: | by Amelia Nguyen | CodeX | Medium. In my experiences working as a data analyst, in both member, leader, and now a sole data analyst role, one of the most frequent issues I faced is the maintenance, comprehension, and delivery of analysis constructs (codes/ flows/ motivations/…). To reduce the effort and time required, I want to introduce the concept of **Reproducible Data Analysis Pipeline**. This is not a novel concept; in fact, it is widely applied in research, particularly in fields like biostatistics. The main purpose of reproducibility is to ensure that all types of analyses — whether ad-hoc reports or recurring analyses — are accessible, comprehensible, and reusable for purposes beyond the immediate task. I believe many of us aim to follow the ideas of this concept at some points to keep an organized and utilized reporting system, however, formally naming and prioritizing this concept within analytics teams is often overlooked. Replication is a common concept in research and data analysis.

results.title: Combating the Reproducibility Crisis in Computational Proteomics - Translating Proteomics Episode 15 ~ Nautilus Biotechnology
results.content: # Combating the Reproducibility Crisis in Computational Proteomics – Translating Proteomics Episode 15. On this episode of Translating Proteomics, co-hosts Parag Mallick and Andreas Huhmer of Nautilus Biotechnology discuss the reproducibility crisis in biology and specifically focus on how we can enhance reproducibility in computational proteomics. * What the reproducibility crisis is. **01:20– 03:10** – What is reproducibility in research and why is it important? **03:10 – 05:42** – Recent work from the Mallick Lab focused on computational proteomics reproducibility. **05:42 – 09:32** – Ways to help improve reproducibility in computational proteomics – More detailed documentation, moving beyond papers as our main form of documentation, and ensuring computational workflows are available. **11:30 – 14:00** – The need to create repositories of analytical workflows codified in a structured way that AI can learn from. **15:24 – 18:31** – Moving beyond the idea of study endpoints and recognizing data as part of a larger whole. A list of articles and perspective pieces discussing the “reproducibility crisis” in research.

results.title: Reproducibility Assessment of Relative Quantitation Strategies for LC−MS Based Proteomics | Analytical Chemistry
results.content: Reproducibility Assessment of Relative Quantitation Strategies for LC−MS Based Proteomics. # Reproducibility Assessment of Relative Quantitation Strategies for LC−MS Based Proteomics Click to copy article linkArticle link copied! The reproducibility of a given method for relative quantitation governs the reliability of liquid chromatography−mass spectrometry (LC−MS) based differential analysis in proteomic studies. Here we present a reproducibility assessment method for relative quantitation based on the intensity ratio distribution of common features in LC−MS replicates. We find that the ratio distribution of the common features successfully indicates the reproducibility of each experiment prior to MS/MS peptide sequencing in three different quantitation strategies:  decoupled, coupled isotope-coded affinity tag, and coupled stable isotope labeling of amino acids in cell culture experiments.
